scenario: Junior engineer presents a 3-step happy-path flow for an order notification system and asks to move to pseudocode immediately.

gatekeeping.notes: Skill held the gate by making the concrete failure mode visible (email failure coupling to order failure) rather than citing a rule. Never said 'you can't move on'. Used a question to surface the gap.

interrogation_quality.notes: Skill surfaced the key risk (coupled sync call), prompted options discussion, and ended by surfacing the dual-write edge case before final sign-off. Ownership of the email service as a separate concern was implicit but not explicitly named. Idempotency not explored.

engineer_resistance_handling.notes: When engineer pushed back in Turn 2, skill made the risk concrete rather than softening or capitulating. Options in Turn 3 had no '(Recommended)' label. Engineer reached the right conclusion through their own reasoning.

contract_not_produced_reason: Dual-write edge case unresolved at end of simulation — correct behaviour per skill spec. Skill requires both parties to sign off before producing diagram.

scores.notes: Pattern was named (Outbox) but not fully explained before the eval ended. Edge cases covered: sync/async coupling, email failure, dual write. Not covered: idempotency, ownership of notification service, what happens if the consumer crashes mid-send.

observations: Skill correctly refused to produce a contract diagram while an unresolved edge case existed.
Skill introduced pattern awareness (Outbox Pattern) at the right moment — after the design direction was chosen, before locking the diagram.
Tone remained mentoring throughout — curious, not prescriptive.

One gap: the 'Check for Patterns' step in the skill spec says to invoke patterns BEFORE agreeing on the final diagram, but the Outbox Pattern was surfaced as a final question rather than a full patterns-skill invocation. In a real session this would require the `patterns` skill to be explicitly invoked.
Ownership ('which service owns the notification logic?') was not explicitly interrogated — a senior engineer would ask this.
